headline: Perno's Debut, and the Night the Roof Fell
story: Dom Perno, captain of UConn's 1964 Elite Eight team and Dee Rowe's top assistant for five seasons, took over in 1977–78, with the Huskies still an independent after the Yankee Conference dropped basketball. His debut was a 73–62 win over Fordham at the Hartford Civic Center on November 26, 1977. Senior guard Joe Whelton (15.3 points per game) and junior forward Jim Abromaitis (14.5 points, 8.8 rebounds) carried the scoring, with Jeff Carr, Dennis Wolff and Randy LaVigne around them. On January 17, 1978, UConn beat UMass 56–49 in Hartford before 4,746 fans; early the next morning the Civic Center's snow-laden roof collapsed into the empty arena, and the Huskies played the rest of their home games away from Hartford. They were 8–6 that night but won only three of their last 12 games, and a 63–57 loss at Fairfield closed an 11–15 season. Whelton finished with 1,337 career points. That fall Perno's first recruits arrived: Corny Thompson and Mike McKay.

key_moments.text: UConn beats Fordham 73–62 at the Hartford Civic Center in Dom Perno's debut as head coach.

headline: Two Freshmen Lead UConn Back to the NCAAs
story: Perno's second season turned on two Connecticut freshmen: Corny Thompson, who had led Middletown High to a 76-game winning streak, and Bridgeport's Mike McKay. Thompson started every game and averaged 18.6 points and 10.0 rebounds, McKay added 15.9 points, and seniors Randy LaVigne and Jeff Carr steadied a team that started 10–2 and lost only once at home. UConn won overtime thrillers over Rutgers (69–67) and Holy Cross (109–102, at Boston Garden), then won eight of its last nine regular-season games, capped by an 80–75 overtime win over Rhode Island in New Haven. At the ECAC New England tournament at the Providence Civic Center, the Huskies routed Boston College 91–74 and beat Rhode Island again, 58–50, to earn the program's first NCAA bid since 1976; Thompson was the tournament MVP and the ECAC's Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year. Seeded fifth in the East, UConn met fourth-seeded Syracuse in Providence on March 10, 1979, a game NBC televised with Dick Enberg and Al McGuire. Perno later recalled his team trailing by 18 and closing to two before losing 89–81. The 21 wins were UConn's most since 1964–65.

headline: Charter Members of the New Big East
story: In 1979–80 UConn became one of the seven charter members of the Big East Conference, alongside Boston College, Georgetown, Providence, St. John's, Seton Hall and Syracuse. The Huskies' first league game was an 89–73 win over Seton Hall on December 22, 1979, and they went 3–3 in the six-game conference schedule. Sophomores Mike McKay (16.7 points) and Corny Thompson (15.8 points, 9.3 rebounds) led the way, with guard Bobby Dulin and senior forward Jim Abromaitis, while Kentucky transfer Chuck Aleksinas sat out the year. A 73–66 loss at Utah in the Utah Classic became a UConn win when Utah forfeited for using an ineligible player, making the final record 20–9. At the first Big East tournament, in Providence, the Huskies beat Boston College 79–68 in the quarterfinals before Syracuse routed them 92–61 in the semifinals. UConn then hosted St. Peter's in the first round of the NIT at the Field House in Storrs and lost, 71–56. Thompson made second-team All-Big East, McKay third team, and freshman Bruce Kuczenski the all-freshman team.

headline: Eleven Straight Wins and a Top-20 Ranking
story: With Chuck Aleksinas, a 6-foot-11 transfer from Kentucky, joining juniors Corny Thompson and Mike McKay, the 1980–81 Huskies won their first 11 games, a run that included a 78–59 win over Syracuse, and climbed to No. 20 in the AP poll in late January. The first loss came by a point, 58–57 at Boston College, but UConn kept knocking off Big East contenders: 69–68 over St. John's in Hartford, 75–73 in overtime over Georgetown, and 65–63 at Syracuse in the new Carrier Dome. The Huskies went 8–6 in the league, lost to Villanova 65–54 in the Big East tournament quarterfinals in Syracuse, then reached the NIT for a second straight year. They won 65–55 at South Florida before Minnesota ended the season 84–66 at the Hartford Civic Center. Thompson (15.0 points, 8.1 rebounds) made first-team All-Big East, Aleksinas (13.8 points on .631 shooting) second team, McKay third team and freshman guard Vern Giscombe the all-freshman team, while freshman point guard Karl Hobbs averaged 4.7 assists. At 20–9, it was UConn's third straight 20-win season.

headline: A Win at Georgetown, Then Heartbreakers
story: Seniors Corny Thompson and Mike McKay led one more fast start. UConn won 14 of its first 17 games, none bigger than a 63–52 win at No. 13 Georgetown on January 20, 1982, against a Hoyas team, featuring freshman Patrick Ewing, that would reach the national championship game. Three days later the Huskies edged Villanova 53–51 in Hartford. Then the close games turned against them: UConn lost eight of its last 11, including a 61–59 loss at Seton Hall and an overtime loss at Villanova, and finished 7–7 in the Big East. With the Big East tournament at the Hartford Civic Center, the Huskies lost 54–52 to St. John's in the quarterfinals, and the season ended with a 76–75 overtime loss at Dayton in the first round of the NIT. Thompson made first-team All-Big East for the second straight year and McKay second team; Thompson finished with 1,810 points and 1,017 rebounds. Their four teams went 78–37, and Thompson, Chuck Aleksinas and McKay were all chosen in the 1982 NBA draft.

headline: Earl Kelley, Big East Freshman of the Year
story: With Corny Thompson, Mike McKay and Chuck Aleksinas graduated, Perno's sixth team leaned on youth, and freshman guard Earl Kelley of New Haven delivered 16.7 points per game and UConn's first Big East Freshman of the Year award. Karl Hobbs (11.8 points), Norman Bailey and Bruce Kuczenski supplied experience. UConn opened 7–2, splitting two games at the Fiesta Classic in Tempe, beating Air Force and Texas A&M to win its own Connecticut Mutual Classic, and winning 71–67 at Pittsburgh in the Panthers' first Big East season. But the new 16-game league schedule was brutal: the Huskies lost 13 of 15 games between January 6 and February 21, most of them to Big East opponents and several to ranked teams. They finished with a flourish, winning at Providence and at Seton Hall and upsetting No. 18 Syracuse 55–54 in Hartford, then lost 69–68 to No. 13 Villanova in the Big East tournament at Madison Square Garden. The 12–16 record was UConn's first losing season since Perno's first year.

headline: Hobbs Leads as Injuries Sideline Earl Kelley
story: Earl Kelley opened his sophomore season scoring freely, but two ankle injuries limited him to 18 games, and the 1983–84 Huskies leaned on 5-foot-8 senior captain Karl Hobbs, who averaged 6.4 assists, made third-team All-Big East and left with a then-school-record 534 career assists. Juniors Alvin Frederick and Ray Broxton, sophomores Eddie Williams and Tim Coles and senior Vern Giscombe rounded out the rotation. UConn went 7–2 before Big East play, beating Columbia and Arizona State to win the Connecticut Mutual Classic, and won three of its first six league games, including a 79–58 rout at Pittsburgh. The schedule then caught up with a thin team. The most memorable night was a loss: an 87–85 triple-overtime defeat at No. 16 Syracuse in the Carrier Dome on February 18, 1984, in which Giscombe played 55 minutes. UConn finished 13–15 and 5–11, losing its last four games, the final one 73–58 to Syracuse in the Big East quarterfinals at Madison Square Garden.

headline: Sweeping Syracuse, Twice by Two Points
story: Junior Earl Kelley returned healthy and averaged 16.8 points and 4.8 assists, earning second-team All-Big East, while seniors Ray Broxton (13.9 points) and Alvin Frederick (11.9) and junior Tim Coles (7.0 rebounds) gave the 1984–85 Huskies a veteran front line. The season opened with a 61–60 loss at Minnesota, and UConn stood 4–7 after an 0–3 start in the Big East. Then came the season's high point: a 70–68 win over No. 7 Syracuse at the Carrier Dome on January 19, 1985. A month later, on February 20, the Huskies beat the seventh-ranked Orangemen again, 71–69 at the Hartford Civic Center, to sweep the season series. UConn also beat Pittsburgh 76–74 and won 74–68 at Boston College, finishing 13–15 and 6–10 in a league that sent Georgetown, St. John's and eventual national champion Villanova to the Final Four. Top-ranked Georgetown ended UConn's season 93–62 in the Big East quarterfinals at Madison Square Garden.

headline: Perno's Last Season: 8–0, Then 4–16
story: Dom Perno's ninth season began with eight straight wins, including a 70–69 win over Minnesota in Hartford and an 84–61 rout of Saint Francis in the opening round of the Connecticut Mutual Classic. The next night, December 28, 1985, Northeastern beat UConn 90–73 in the tournament final at the Hartford Civic Center; Northeastern's coach, Jim Calhoun, would be UConn's next. Senior Earl Kelley averaged 19.6 points and 6.4 assists, but the Huskies won only four of their last 20 games. In mid-February Kelley, the team's leading scorer for four straight seasons, was dismissed from the team for academic reasons, and UConn lost its last eight games, the final one 76–66 to Seton Hall in the first round of the Big East tournament, to finish 12–16 and 3–13. Kelley still made second-team All-Big East and was drafted by the San Antonio Spurs, and freshmen Phil Gamble, an all-freshman pick, and 6-foot-10 Cliff Robinson offered a glimpse of the future. On April 14, 1986, after four straight losing seasons, Perno resigned with a 139–114 record; a month later UConn hired Calhoun.
